oneSentence: A mechanism that lets each token reweight information from available tokens in the same sequence, including itself, before the next layer processes it.
plainExplanation:
Self-attention is a way for a model to compute how strongly information from parts of one sequence should contribute at each position. A sequence can be a sentence, code tokens, image patches, or other ordered pieces of input. For every token, the model produces a new representation: a numeric description that mixes information from that token and from other available tokens.

The input is a sequence of token representations, often called embeddings. For each token, the model creates three derived vectors: a query, a key and a value. A vector is an ordered list of numbers. The query from one token is compared with the keys of available tokens to get attention scores. Higher scores give information from those tokens more influence at this step.

Those scores are turned into weights, usually so they add up to 1 across the available tokens. The model then builds a weighted sum of the value vectors. That weighted sum forms the self-attention output for the token being processed. This happens for every token, so each token can gain context from distant as well as nearby tokens.

This is called self-attention because the queries, keys and values come from the same sequence. That differs from cross-attention, where one sequence attends to a different sequence, such as a decoder attending to an encoder output. It is also not the same as attention in the broad sense: self-attention is one specific attention pattern used inside transformers.

everydayAnalogy.title: Matching a photographed form to the right template
everydayAnalogy.story: A clerk in Lima receives a phone photo of a paper form. To identify each blurred field, the clerk compares one field at a time with every field on the standard template: the position of the date, the shape of the ID box, the nearby label and the spacing around it. For the field that looks like a date, the clerk gives more weight to template regions that match those clues and less weight to unrelated regions such as the signature line. The clerk then combines those stronger matches to decide how to label that field in context, not just by its isolated appearance.

mapping.analogyElement: one field in the photographed form being checked
mapping.aiElement: one token whose representation is being updated

mapping.analogyElement: comparing that field with all template fields
mapping.aiElement: comparing one query with all keys in the sequence

mapping.analogyElement: stronger and weaker matches across template regions

mapping.aiElement: weighted sum of value vectors to form a new representation

everydayAnalogy.limitation: The analogy compares an image to a separate template, but self-attention usually works within one sequence attending to itself, not to an external reference. A clerk may use explicit rules such as 'dates look like this', while self-attention uses learned numeric projections. Also, real self-attention updates all positions in parallel and produces continuous vectors, not human-readable labels at each step.

visual.title: How one token gathers context from the whole sequence
visual.learningObjective: After using this explainer, a reader should be able to say how one token compares itself with all tokens, turns match strengths into weights, and combines their information into a new representation.
visual.description: An interactive sequence of tokens is shown in a row. Selecting a focus token highlights lines from its query to every token's key, with line thickness showing score strength. A second panel shows the normalised weights and the resulting weighted mix of value vectors. The reader can switch examples, move the focus token, and compare before and after representations.

steps.label: Choose a focus token
steps.explanation: Select one token in the sequence. The explainer treats that token's query as the current question: which other tokens are relevant to updating this position?
steps.visualInstruction: Render tokens as clickable pills in a horizontal row. When selected, outline the focus token and label its vector as Q. Show each token's K and V labels beneath or in a tooltip.

steps.label: Compare with every token
steps.explanation: The focus token's query is compared with every token's key, including its own. The result is a score for each possible source of information.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw SVG connectors from the focus token to all tokens. Encode larger scores with thicker, darker lines and show numeric score badges above each destination token.

steps.label: Turn scores into weights
steps.explanation: The scores are converted into weights so they can be used as proportions. Larger scores become larger weights, but all weights together sum to 1.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a bar chart aligned to the tokens. Animate or update bars from raw scores to normalised weights, with a total indicator reading 1.00.

steps.label: Mix value vectors
steps.explanation: Each token's value vector contributes according to its weight. The weighted combination becomes the updated representation for the focus token.
steps.visualInstruction: Display small stacked segments or numeric multipliers beside each value vector, then show them combining into one output vector for the focus token.

steps.label: Compare before and after
steps.explanation: The updated representation now carries information from other relevant tokens. The token stays in the same position, but its numeric description has changed.
steps.visualInstruction: Place the original embedding and the new contextual representation side by side, with changed dimensions highlighted.

visual.interaction: The reader can choose among short example sequences, click any token to make it the focus, and toggle views for scores, normalised weights and the final weighted sum. A reset button returns to the default example.
visual.accessibilityDescription: Screen-reader version: You hear a sequence of tokens, then choose one as the focus. For that token, the interface reads a list of comparison scores against every token in order, followed by the normalised weights that sum to 1. It then states that the output for the focus token is formed by multiplying each token's value vector by its weight and adding the results. A final summary compares the original token representation with the new context-aware representation and explains which tokens influenced it most.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Reduced-motion version: no animated lines or transitions. The same example appears as a static table with columns for token, score, weight and weighted value contribution, plus a fixed side-by-side view of the original and updated representation for the selected token.

workedExample.scenario: In the sentence "The catalogue entry was returned to the focal point because it was incomplete", examine the token "it".
workedExample.input: Tokens: [The, catalogue, entry, was, returned, to, the, focal, point, because, it, was, incomplete]
process: The layer projects every token representation into a query, key and value. The query for "it" is compared with the keys for all allowed tokens, including its own key.

For one illustrative attention head, the normalised weights might assign 0.30 to "entry", 0.25 to "incomplete", 0.12 to "catalogue", 0.08 to "it", 0.07 to "returned", and 0.18 across the remaining tokens.

The representation for "it" becomes a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors. Information from "entry" and "incomplete" therefore contributes more strongly than information from "focal point".
A residual connection typically combines this attention output with the token's earlier representation before the result passes to subsequent processing.
workedExample.result: The position of "it" is unchanged, but its updated representation now carries evidence that it refers more strongly to the catalogue entry than to the focal point.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At the annual workplan review, an ombudsman case officer in a documentation and library service uses an approved drafting tool to revise a non-sensitive paragraph on records management. Self-attention allows each token to draw on other tokens in the paragraph, so a phrase such as "the revised filing procedure" can influence the later word "it" even when several words intervene.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The mechanism helps explain how a transformer keeps references, qualifications and defined terms connected across a sentence. It does not retrieve the correct interpretation from a file. It reweights token representations within the sequence presented to it.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Ombudsman case files, identities, allegations, correspondence and associated metadata must not be entered into a tool unless it is explicitly approved for that material. Such information is confidential and may expose individuals or compromise a case. Keep the exercise to non-sensitive administrative text and review the output before clearance.

whyItMatters: Self-attention helps explain why transformers work well on language, code and other sequences. For a non-specialist, this matters because it shows what the model is actually doing: not retrieving one exact rule, but repeatedly reweighting parts of the input to build context-aware representations. That helps you judge strengths and limits. A system using self-attention may capture long-range relationships better than older sequence models, but it can still miss meaning, rely on weak patterns or spread errors through the representation. Knowing this supports better choices about procurement, evaluation, safety checks and when human review is needed.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Self-attention means the model looks only at the most important word.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not usually. Each output token is built from a weighted mixture of all tokens, not a single winner. Some weights may be large and many small, but the mechanism is generally a soft combination across the sequence.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Self-attention and attention are the same term.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Self-attention is one specific kind of attention. The general term attention covers several patterns. In self-attention, queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, they do not.

By itself, self-attention compares token representations without an inherent notion of sequence order. Transformer systems therefore add position information, often through positional encodings or related methods, so the model can distinguish 'A before B' from 'B before A'.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A high attention weight proves a model's reasoning or explanation.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Attention weights show how information is mixed at one step of computation. They can be useful clues, but they are not a complete or universally accepted explanation of why the full model produced a final output.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Each token draws more information from the available tokens in the same input that receive higher computed weights.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Given input token representations X, the layer learns projections that produce Q, K and V. For each position i, it computes similarity scores between q_i and every allowed k_j, scales and normalises them into weights, and uses those weights to form a weighted sum of the corresponding v_j. The result is a contextualised representation for position i. Doing this for every position gives a full set of updated token representations. In transformers, this is typically wrapped with residual connections, layer normalisation and feed-forward sublayers. Self-attention describes where Q, K and V come from. Multi-head attention describes running several attention heads in parallel, so multi-head attention can perform self-attention.

keyTakeaway: Self-attention lets each token rebuild its representation from a weighted combination of all tokens it is allowed to attend to, including itself, before the next layer processes it.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes self-attention in a transformer?
options: Each token creates a new representation by weighting information from all tokens in the same sequence.
The model chooses one earlier token and copies its value into the current position.
The mechanism sorts tokens by importance once for the whole sentence and keeps that order fixed.
It is the same as multi-head attention, except used only during training.
quickCheck.explanation: In self-attention, each position compares its query with keys from available positions in the same sequence, obtains weights, and forms a weighted mixture of their value vectors. The weights can differ by position. Cross-attention uses a separate source sequence, while multi-head attention describes running several heads in parallel.

issues.problem: The page repeatedly says each token attends to every token or the full sequence. That is not generally true when self-attention is masked or otherwise restricted. The one-sentence definition and simple explanation also say "other tokens", incorrectly excluding the token itself. Self-attention can include the token's own key and value.
issues.fix: Use "available tokens in the same sequence, including itself" in general definitions. Present the visual as an unmasked example, or show unavailable positions with zero weight.

issues.problem: The model is said to "decide which parts ... matter most". This presents a mental act as fact. The mechanism computes scores and weights from learned projections.
issues.fix: Replace this with "compute how strongly information from parts of that sequence should contribute at each position".

Treating the six "near 0" scores as 0 gives exp(3.2)=24.5325, exp(2.7)=14.8797, exp(1.5)=4.4817, exp(1.1)=3.0042, exp(0.8)=2.2255, and 6×exp(0)=6. The total is 55.1236. The listed remaining weight of 0.23 would require the omitted scores to be around 0.9, not near 0. The calculation is al
issues.fix: Change "others near 0" to "each other score is 0". Then use: "After softmax normalisation, the weights are approximately: animal 0.45, tired 0.27, it 0.08, road 0.05, because 0.04, and remaining tokens 0.11 combined."

issues.problem: The final sentence falsely treats self-attention and multi-head attention as alternatives. They describe different properties. Self-attention describes the source of queries, keys and values. Multi-head attention describes running several attention heads in parallel. A multi-head layer can perform self-attention.
issues.fix: Replace the final sentence with: "Self-attention describes where Q, K and V come from. Multi-head attention describes running several attention heads in parallel, so multi-head attention can perform self-attention."

issues.problem: Option 0 is the intended answer, but its claim that information comes from "all tokens" is not correct for restricted or masked self-attention. Option 1 is false because the output is normally a weighted mixture, not one copied earlier value. Option 2 is false because weights are computed separately for each position. Option 3 is false because self-attention can be multi-head and is used beyond training. The last three are also exaggerated enough that the answer is obvious without understanding the term.
issues.fix: Use these options: ["Each token creates a new representation by weighting information from available tokens in the same sequence.", "Every token uses one shared set of weights over the sequence.", "Each token weights information from a separate input sequence.", "Several attention patterns run in parallel, regardless of where their inputs come from."] Keep correctOptionIndex as 0 and revise the explanation accordingly.

issues.problem: The analogy's central action compares a photographed form with a separate template. That models cross-attention, the exact mechanism this page needs to distinguish from self-attention. The limitation admits the mismatch, but the story and mapping still teach the wrong source relationship.
issues.fix: Keep the comparison within one photographed form. Have the clerk interpret one blurred field by comparing it with labels, values and layout elsewhere on that same form. Map all compared fields to tokens in one sequence.
